# Background

To understand the design principles behind Mojo and the improvements it brings,
it is first essential to understand the compiler infrastructure it is built on.
Mojo is implemented directly on top of MLIR, which itself builds on the original
LLVM IR. Understanding how IR works, where it falls short, and how MLIR
addresses those shortcomings is what gives context to Mojo's key properties,
which allow it to elegantly address both the two-language split and vendor
lock-in.

## LLVM [@lattnerLLVMCompilationFramework2004]

LLVM is a compiler framework designed to normalize code representation across
languages, making it possible to apply a shared set of optimizations to any
code compiled with it [@lattnerLLVMCompilationFramework2004]. To achieve this,
LLVM represents programs in Static Single Assignment (SSA) form, where each
variable is defined exactly once. This representation, called LLVM Intermediate
Representation (LLVM IR), abstracts away language-specific constructs and
reduces code to raw semantics, allowing the same optimization passes to work
across C, C++, Rust, Swift, and many other languages. IR is often
described as roughly C with vectors [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020],
operating at a single fixed abstraction level. This means both high-level
language features and machine-specific details are out of scope. To illustrate,
consider the matrix multiplication below.

```c
for (int i = 0; i < N; i++)
  for (int j = 0; j < N; j++)
    for (int k = 0; k < N; k++)
      C[i][j] += A[i][k] * B[k][j];
```

Compiled to IR, the loop structure disappears entirely into control flow.
What remains is raw pointer arithmetic operating on individual memory addresses. Each `%` assignment is an
instance of SSA.

```llvm
%a_p  = getelementptr float, float* %A, i64 %a_i
%a_v  = load float, float* %a_p
%b_p  = getelementptr float, float* %B, i64 %b_i
%b_v  = load float, float* %b_p
%prod = fmul float %a_v, %b_v
%c_p  = getelementptr float, float* %C, i64 %c_i
%c_v  = load float, float* %c_p
%sum  = fadd float %c_v, %prod
store float %sum, float* %c_p
```

the compiler can optimise individual operations but has lost the information that this is a matrix multiply, what the memory layout is, or that the loops are parallelisable

As stated in the original LLVM paper, LLVM is not intended to be a universal
compiler IR and does not represent high-level language features directly, nor
does it capture machine-dependent features or code sequences used by back-end
code generators [@lattnerLLVMCompilationFramework2004]. This works well for
CPU-targeted, homogeneous compilation but becomes a limiting factor when
targeting heterogeneous hardware or domain-specific optimizations. Many problems
are simply better modeled at a different abstraction level, for example
source-level analysis of C++ code is very difficult on IR
[@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]. As a result, languages like Swift,
Rust, and Julia each ended up building their own mid-level IRs before targeting
LLVM, leading to fragmented and duplicated compiler infrastructure with each
team reimplementing the same class of optimizations
[@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020], as illustrated in @fig-llvm.

![Compilation pipeline of different languages with multiple mid-level IRs for language-specific optimization with common backend for multiple hardware targets [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]](images/LLVM_intermediate_IR.png){#fig-llvm width=90%}

## MLIR [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]

### Motivation

- ML and HPC compiler stacks were deeply fragmented as a direct consequence of
  LLVM's fixed abstraction level
- frameworks like TensorFlow were "composed of many different compilers, graph
  technologies, and runtime systems" with no shared infrastructure
  [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- this "manifested in multiple user-visible ways, including poor error messages,
  failures in edge cases, unpredictable performance, and difficulty generalizing
  the stack to support new hardware" [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- MLIR was developed to solve this by making it cheap to define new abstraction
  levels within a single, shared compiler infrastructure

### Core Idea

- multi-level IR: multiple abstraction levels coexist in one framework
- "little builtin, everything customizable" [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- the system is based on a minimal number of fundamental concepts, with most of the
  intermediate representation left fully customizable
- contrast with LLVM's one-size-fits-all approach: "a single abstraction level to
  interface with the system" [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]

### Dialects

- logical groupings of operations, types, and attributes under a unique namespace
- "MLIR explicitly supports a mix of dialects to enable progressive lowering. Ops from
  different dialects can coexist at any level of the IR at any time" [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- adding support for a new hardware target means defining a new lowering dialect
- enables reuse across domains, for example an OpenMP dialect shared between Fortran
  and C frontends [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]

### Progressive Lowering

- "the system should support progressive lowering, i.e. from the higher-level
  representation down to the lowest-level, with the lowering being performed in small
  steps along multiple abstraction levels" [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- "the need for multiple levels of abstractions stems from the variety of platforms
  and programming models that a generic compiler infrastructure has to support"
  [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- contrast with rigid pipelines: Clang lowers from ASTs to LLVM IR, to SelectionDAG,
  to MachineInstr, and to MCInst in a fixed sequence. Compiler passes can only
  operate at one level at a time [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- crucially, MLIR allows *different parts of the IR to sit at different abstraction
  levels simultaneously*: "mixing different levels of abstractions and different
  concepts in the same IR is a key property of the system to allow a part of the
  representation to remain in higher-level abstraction while another part is lowered"
  [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- this means a compiler for a custom accelerator can, for instance, reuse high-level
  loop structure alongside primitive scalar/vector instructions specific to that
  accelerator, in the same IR at the same time [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]

### SSA and Nested Regions

- MLIR extends the standard SSA form with *nested regions* as a first-class concept:
  operations contain regions, regions contain blocks, blocks contain operations.
  This recursive structure lifts higher-level abstractions (loops, closures,
  parallel constructs) directly into the IR at any abstraction level
  [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]
- instead of φ-nodes, MLIR uses block arguments passed by terminator operations,
  which composes cleanly across nesting levels
- the same matrix multiplication expressed in MLIR's affine dialect preserves the
  loop structure as nested regions, each being a first-class scope with its own
  SSA values and control flow:

```mlir
affine.for %i = 0 to %N {
  affine.for %j = 0 to %N {
    %0 = affine.load %A[%i]   : memref<?xf32>
    %1 = affine.load %B[%j]   : memref<?xf32>
    %2 = mulf %0, %1           : f32
    %3 = affine.load %C[%i,%j] : memref<?x?xf32>
    %4 = addf %3, %2           : f32
    affine.store %4, %C[%i,%j] : memref<?x?xf32>
  }
}
```

- the loop body lives inside the operation as a region, not as a separate function.
  The compiler can therefore analyse and transform loop structure without losing
  the surrounding context [@lattnerMLIRCompilerInfrastructure2020]


### Why This Matters for Portability

- the same high-level representation can be lowered to different hardware backends
  by swapping the lowering dialect, keeping abstractions hardware-agnostic at the
  top and hardware-specific at the bottom
- Mojo is the first language built directly on MLIR, inheriting these properties
